headline: Bunker Schools Push the Point — and We're Two Days Into the Albie Watch
subhead: Stripers and bluefish are stacked on peanut bunker from the Lighthouse to Shagwong, and the tide behind the new moon is setting up exactly what we said it would.
body_markdown:
I've been standing on that boulder field below the Lighthouse since I was tall enough to see over the rocks, and there's a particular kind of August morning that tells you the season is about to turn. This is one of them. The bunker showed up thick this week — not the scattered pods we saw in July, but real, wide schools stacking off the north side and rolling around the Point on the tide change. Where the bunker go, everything else follows, and right now everything else means striped bass, jumbo bluefish, and a whole lot of nervous water.

The blitz activity has been visible from North Bar out past Shagwong Reef, and it's been consistent enough that I'm comfortable calling it the story of the week. Bass are busting bunker on top in that classic August pattern — slot fish mixed with a real number of overslot bass in the 30-to-40-inch class, working the edges of the bait balls where the current bends around structure. I had one morning on the incoming where three separate boils opened up within casting range of the boulder field, and every one of them produced. A 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 1-ounce bucktail got bit the second it hit bottom, but the better bite came on bunker spoons and topwater — a Hogy Pencil worked right through the froth pulled fish that never would've looked at a subtler presentation. If you want to go old school, a whole bunker on a fishfinder rig, fished dead-drift right on the edge of the boil, still puts big bass in the boat. Depths have been running 15 to 30 feet on the drops around the Point, tighter to the rocks on the building tide, then sliding out toward deeper water as the flow eases.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on this whole pattern, and I mean serious bluefish — not the snappers you're seeing in the harbors, but 8-to-12-pound choppers that'll shred a bucktail trailer in one pass. If you're fishing wire or heavier mono leader you're in business. If you're running straight braid to a soft plastic, budget for losses.

South side, the fluke bite has held up better than I expected for mid-August. The bigger tides this week pulled bait and moved fish, and I've heard of doormat-class fluke coming out of the deeper drifts off the ocean beaches — fish pushing past 6 pounds on white Gulp paired with a heavier bucktail, 3/4 to 1 ounce depending on how hard the current's running. The pattern's been the same all season: work the drift slow, keep bottom contact, and don't be afraid to switch to a bigger bait when the current picks up on the outgoing. It's not a five-fish limit every trip, but the quality has been there for anyone putting in the drift time.

Now to the story everybody at the dock has been talking about. We flagged this last week — said the albie and bonito push would trigger around the August 12 new moon as the tidal current built and started shoving bait harder through the rips. We're two days past that moon now, and the current is doing exactly what it needed to do. Squid have been building steadily to our east around Rhode Island and Nantucket, and that's the trigger that usually pulls the first wave of speedsters down into our rips. I haven't gotten a confirmed albie in hand yet myself, but the water's right — 69 degrees off the Point, clean, with good bait density — and every captain I've talked to at the dock this week is rigging Epoxy Jigs and small Deadly Dick lures just in case that first sighting comes off the east side near Frisco Grounds or out toward Shagwong. If you're heading out this weekend, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a 7/8-ounce metal ready to go alongside your bass gear. When it happens, it happens fast, and you don't want to be re-tying while the school's still up.

I want to be straight with you about one thing — this bunker bite, as good as it looks from a distance, has been patchy in practice. Some mornings the boils are everywhere and every cast connects. Other mornings the bunker have pushed off the structure entirely and you're running the shoreline burning gas looking for the next pod. The wind's played a role — a stiff southwest breeze the last few days has pushed some of that surface activity west of where I'd expect it this time of year, so don't assume the fish will be sitting in the same spot two days running. Cover water, watch the birds, and trust moving bait over a static spot.

Looking ahead, I expect this bass-and-blue bunker pattern to hold through the week as long as the bait stays put, and if the current keeps building the way it has, I'd put real money on Montauk producing the first confirmed albie or bonito of the season before this week is out. That's the moment everyone out here waits for — when the Point flips from summer pattern into that electric stretch that carries us into the fall run. It's close. I can feel it in the water.
